chain.g: to mount up to, come up to, signify

ety.text: Old French amonterbor. Middle English amounten English amount From Middle English amounten (“to mount up to, come up to, signify”), from Old French amonter (“to amount to”), from amont, amunt (“uphill, upward”), from the prepositional phrase a mont (“toward or to a mountain or heap”), from Latin ad montem, from ad (“to”) + montem, accusative of mons (“mountain”).

senses.d: The total, aggregate or sum of material (not applicable to discrete numbers or units or items in standard English).
ex: The amount of atmospheric pollution threatens a health crisis.

senses.d: A quantity or volume.
ex: Pour a small amount of water into the dish.
The dogs need different amounts of food.

senses.d: The number (the sum) of elements in a set.
ex: The final amount of students who have participated to mobility for the period 1995-1999 is held to be around 460 000.

senses.d: To total or evaluate.
ex: The money in my pocket amounts to three dollars and change.

senses.d: To be the tantamount to; to reach up to the level of.
ex: He was a pretty good student, but never amounted to much professionally.
His response amounted to gross insubordination.

senses.d: To go up; to ascend.
ex: So up he rose, and thence amounted straight.

Proto-Indo-European *ḱóm Proto-Germanic *ga- Proto-West Germanic *ga- Old English ġe- Old English mang Old English ġemang Old English onġemang Old English amang Middle English among English among The preposition is derived from Middle English among, amang, amange, amonge (“in the presence of, amid, among; in, within; between; during”), from Old English amang, onġemang (preposition), from on (“on, among, in”) (probably ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₂en- (“on, onto”)) + ġema…

senses.d: Of a person or thing: in the midst of and surrounded by (other people or things).
ex: to put the cat among the pigeons
And Adam hyd him ſelf with his wyfe [Eve], from the preſence of yͤ LORDE God amonge the trees of the garden.

senses.d: Associated with or living alongside (other people or things).
ex: How can you speak with authority about their customs when you have never lived among them?
In like maner Ephraim droue not out yͤ Cananites that dwelt at Gaſer [Gezer], but the Cananites dwelt amonge them at Gaſer.

senses.d: Belonging to (a group comprising similar people or things).
ex: He is among the few who completely understand the subject.
All this has led to an explosion of protest across China, including among a middle class that has discovered nimbyism.

senses.d: Distinct in some way from (other members of a group); specifically, superior or pre-eminent compared to (other members of a group).
Originally, in the course of; during; now, in the circumstances or context of.
Distributed or divided between (members of a group).
ex: And if you come hether, / When Damſines [damsons] I gether, / I will part them all you among.
There is a lad here, which hath fiue barley loaues, and two ſmall fiſhes: but what are they among ſo many?

senses.d: Done jointly by (two or more people).
ex: [Y]ou haue among you, kild a ſvveet and innocent lady: […]

senses.d: In the general custom or opinion of (members of a group).
Occurring between (members of a group) or within (a group).
ex: Lactose intolerance is common among people of Asian heritage.
Then was there diſcenſion amõge [amonge] the Jewes for theſe ſayenges.

senses.d: Along with (someone or something); together.
ex: Yeat interlace vve ſhall among the Loue of her and him: […]

senses.d: At the same time, all the while, meanwhile.
In addition, beside.
Chiefly with contrasting adjectives or adverbs: from time to time, now and then; also, here and there.
ex: [Y[our beſt vvay is, to direct your courſe Eaſt North-eaſt, and North-eaſt by Eaſt, among; […]
